An evaluator can often afford to run a new model on only $k$ of the $N$ benchmarks a leaderboard holds. We ask which $k$ to run, how to infer the rest, and how large $k$ must be, on 238 embedding models and 328 MTEB tasks and on 4{,}507 open language models and 39 Open LLM Leaderboard subtasks, holding out whole organisations or families and scoring every method on benchmarks that no selection rule can choose. A factor model with a greedy design criterion beats random selection by about 1.9 points of RMSE when two or three MTEB benchmarks are run and, at a margin of a quarter of the floor, is equivalent to it from about eight (three to five of 39 on the leaderboard); no other inference rule we tried beats it by more than that margin. On MTEB, eight benchmarks bring the error within 2 points of what the model's other scores give, 32 to 50 within 1 point, and none resolves neighbouring models: the floor is about 5 points, 2.5 times what the model predicts, for a cause we do not find. On the leaderboard that factor is 1.1 for held-out families and 2.5 for the strongest quarter. A rule that reads $k$ from the training models alone matches the measured $k$ within one grid step when whole groups are held out, and not under a shift in strength or time.

cd /hutian/repo; cat > paper/abstract.tex <<'EOF'
An evaluator can often afford to run a new model on only $k$ of the $N$ benchmarks a leaderboard holds. We ask which $k$ to run, how to infer the rest, and how large $k$ must be, on 238 embedding models and 328 MTEB tasks and on 4{,}507 open language models and 39 Open LLM Leaderboard subtasks, holding out whole organisations or families and scoring every method on benchmarks that no selection rule can choose. The error cannot fall below a floor, the error of predicting a model's scores when all its other observed scores are given: about 5 points on MTEB. A factor model with a greedy design criterion beats random selection by about 1.9 points of RMSE when two or three MTEB benchmarks are run and is practically equivalent to it (within a quarter of the floor) from about eight, and on the leaderboard from five of 39 (families) or eight (strongest quarter); on MTEB no other inference rule we tried beats it by more than that margin. On MTEB, eight benchmarks bring the error within 2 points of the floor, 32 to 50 within 1 point, and none resolves neighbouring models; the floor is 2.5 times what the model predicts, for a cause we do not find. On the leaderboard that factor is 1.1 for held-out families and 2.5 for the strongest quarter. A rule that reads $k$ from the training models alone matches the measured $k$ within one grid step when whole groups are held out, and not under a shift in strength or time.

\section{Related work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Cheaper evaluation within one benchmark.}
tinyBenchmarks~\citep{polo2024tinybenchmarks}, metabench~\citep{kipnis2024metabench} and anchor points~\citep{vivek2024anchor} choose \emph{examples} of one benchmark so that its full score can be recovered. We choose \emph{whole benchmarks} and predict \emph{other} benchmarks, so the target is not a function of what was run.

\paragraph{Low-dimensional structure of model scores.}
Observational scaling laws~\citep{ruan2024observational} and Sloth~\citep{polo2024sloth} find that scores of language models lie near a low-dimensional capability space and use it to extrapolate across models and families; neither asks which $k$ benchmarks to run for a new model or how large $k$ must be. Agreement between benchmarks depends on analysis choices~\citep{perlitz2024benchbench}, so our protocol fixes the matrix definition and the margins before any result.

\paragraph{Cold-start elicitation and matrix completion.}
Which items to ask a new user to rate is the cold-start problem of recommenders~\citep{rashid2002getting,golbandi2011adaptive,elahi2016survey,houlsby2014coldstart}; a new model is a new user, a benchmark an item. Probabilistic PCA with missing data~\citep{tipping1999ppca} supplies our inference model. Matrix-completion theory~\citep{candes2009exact,candes2010power,mazumder2010spectral} assumes the observed entries are sampled at random, whereas here the new row's observed set is \emph{chosen}.

\paragraph{Optimal design and adaptive testing.}
Choosing columns to predict the rest is column subset selection~\citep{boutsidis2009css}; greedy selection carries guarantees through the submodularity ratio~\citep{das2011submodular,bian2017guarantees} and Bayesian experimental design~\citep{chaloner1995bayesian}, and multidimensional adaptive testing selects items by such criteria~\citep{mulder2009multidimensional}. We claim no new selection method; we add the measured answer on real leaderboard matrices with missing cells and whole models held out, a decomposition of the error, and the conditions under which the answer holds.

Version 1 is now in `release`: I merged `paper-repo`#7 after `internal-review-repo` approved it. It covers MTEB only, so the paper is not yet in `final`.

On `dev`, which is pushed and has no undefined references in my local build:
- **Abstract:** rewritten. It defines the floor at first use, names one margin, and states the leaderboard result as "from five (families) or eight (strongest quarter) of 39". The inference-rule claim is now limited to MTEB.

- **Theory:** the terms "noise" and ‖v‖² are now defined.
- **Idea request:** I opened `idea-repo`#10 asking for related work on score prediction across LLM benchmarks and IRT-based evaluation. This is the review's "may" finding.

The main text still runs past page 9, by about 16 lines. `figtab-repo`'s shorter Fig. 3 and `fig3c_estimation_vs_M.pdf` are on its `main` but not yet on `dev`. I asked for delivery in `paper-repo`#8, together with the cramped k/N label on Fig. 1a. Once they arrive I'll update the Fig. 3 panel letters and add `fig3c` to appendix C.

I'll then cut the next candidate for the owners to review and reply on `paper-repo`#6 and #9.
